claims.claim: AI stories state their themes outright far more often than human stories (explicit narrator thematic commentary 77% vs 52%).
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Iyyer & Wieting, StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136, Apr 2026)
claims.quote: AI stories over-explain themes and favor tidy, single-track plots

claims.claim: AI stories run one plot line with no subplots 79% of the time versus 57% for human stories.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)

claims.claim: AI stories express emotion through bodily-response description in 81% of stories versus 38% of human stories.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)

claims.claim: AI stories reach for smell imagery in 82% of stories versus 57% of human stories.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)

claims.claim: AI stories resolve through the protagonist's own action 69% of the time versus 46% for humans, and end ambiguously less often.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)

claims.claim: Human protagonists' choices are framed as morally ambiguous in 59% of stories versus 38% of AI stories.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)
claims.quote: frame protagonist' choices as more morally ambiguous

claims.claim: Human stories use chronological discontinuity, fourth-wall breaks (67% vs 39%), direct reader address (28% vs 7%) and named intertextual references (47% vs 24%) far more than AI stories.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)

claims.claim: AI stories cluster in a shared region of narrative-feature space (human–AI centroid distance 1.6x AI–AI; 24.7% of human stories in the rarest decile vs 7.1% of AI).
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)
claims.quote: occupy a rarer, more dispersed region of narrative space

claims.claim: Narrative-level features still identify AI fiction at 93.9% macro-F1 after professional-style rewriting, so surface edits do not humanize structure.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)
claims.quote: far harder to humanize

claims.claim: Each model family has a signature: Claude's event intensity escalates less, GPT over-uses gossip and dream sequences, Gemini writes the tidiest endings.
claims.source: Russell et al., StoryScope (arXiv 2604.03136)
claims.quote: Claude produces notably flat event escalation

claims.claim: LLM-processed text shows abrupt excess of style words such as delves (28x), showcasing (10x), intricate, underscores, pivotal, meticulously, realm; 2024 excess words were 66% verbs and 16% adjectives.
claims.source: Kobak, González-Márquez, Horvát & Lause (arXiv 2406.07016; Science Advances 2025)

claims.feature: lexical overuse not inherited from training data
claims.claim: Twenty-one focal words (delve, showcasing, underscores, intricate, garnered, boasts, groundbreaking, realm, aligns, etc.) are overrepresented in ChatGPT output yet not in pre-LLM corpora, consistent with RLHF as the source.
claims.source: Juzek & Ward, Why Does ChatGPT Delve So Much? (arXiv 2412.11385, Dec 2024)
claims.quote: Lexical overrepresentation remains a feature of current iterations of ChatGPT

claims.claim: Readers become wary of signature words like delve and may judge a text on those words rather than its content.
claims.source: Juzek & Ward (arXiv 2412.11385)
claims.quote: wary of the word 'delve'

claims.claim: Professional New Yorker stories pass 84.7% of 14 expert creativity tests; LLM stories pass 9% (GPT-3.5) to 30% (Claude 1.3).
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Laban, Agarwal, Muresan & Wu, Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024; arXiv 2309.14556)
claims.quote: three to ten times less likely to pass individual TTCW

claims.claim: LLM stories almost never pass Originality in Form (0–8.3% vs 63.9%) or Originality in Theme & Content (0–19.4% vs 75%).
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024)

claims.claim: LLM stories pass Rhetorical Complexity only 2.8–11.1% of the time (humans 88.9%) and Literary Devices 5.6–36.1% (humans 88.9%).
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024)
claims.quote: Attempts at figurative language come across as overwrought, confusing, nonsensical.

claims.claim: Expert writers report that LLM figurative language lacks subtlety and obscures rather than illuminates.
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024)
claims.quote: Subtlety and restraint seem lacking

claims.claim: LLM stories pass the Narrative Ending test 8.3–33.3% of the time versus 91.7% for professionals; experts flag moralistic, unearned and unrealistically happy resolutions.
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024)
claims.quote: Abrupt or unearned resolutions, overly moralistic conclusions, unrealistic happy endings

claims.claim: LLM stories lean on summary/exposition instead of dramatized scene (pass 8.3–58.3% vs 91.7%).
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024)
claims.quote: Overreliance on summary leaves the narrative ungrounded

claims.claim: LLM stories pass Character Development 8.3–16.7% (humans 61.1%) and Perspective & Voice Flexibility 8.3–19.4% (humans 72.2%).
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024)

claims.claim: A story can avoid clichéd phrasing yet still fail originality because its ideas and themes are stock.
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024), expert explanation on a Claude story
claims.quote: its ideas and themes are hackneyed

claims.claim: No LLM judge positively correlated with expert creativity assessments of the same stories.
claims.source: Chakrabarty et al., Art or Artifice? (CHI 2024)
claims.quote: None of the LLMs positively correlate with the expert assessments

claims.claim: Across 60 LLMs vs 60 humans, human five-sentence stories are more novel, more surprising and more lexically and semantically diverse (p<0.05 to p<0.0001).
claims.source: Ismayilzada, Stevenson & van der Plas (ICCC 2025; arXiv 2411.02316)
claims.quote: fall short in terms of novelty, surprise and diversity

claims.claim: LLM stories are more linguistically complex and verbose (more unique words, longer dependency paths, more nouns and adjectives) but less creative than human stories.
claims.source: Ismayilzada et al. (ICCC 2025)
claims.quote: linguistically more complex and verbose yet less creative

claims.claim: Experts rate human stories 1.25 points higher than LLM stories while non-experts rate LLM stories 1.19 points higher and LLM judges 1.85 higher; lay ratings track word count.
claims.source: Ismayilzada et al. (ICCC 2025)
claims.quote: driven by linguistic complexity of the stories

claims.claim: Writers given GPT-4 story ideas produced stories 10.7% more similar to one another and 5.2% more similar to the AI prompts, while individual ratings rose mostly for low-creativity writers.
claims.source: Doshi & Hauser, Science Advances 10(28), 2024
claims.quote: collectively a narrower scope of novel content is produced

claims.claim: People cannot detect AI-written self-presentations and rely on cues (first person, contractions, family topics) that AI can exploit to seem more human than humans.
claims.source: Jakesch, Hancock & Naaman, PNAS 120(11), 2023
claims.quote: intuitive but flawed heuristics

claims.claim: Burrows' Delta on most-frequent words shows LLM stories clustering tightly by model while human stories spread widely; newer GPT-4 is tighter than GPT-3.5.
claims.source: O'Sullivan, Humanities & Social Sciences Communications 12 (2025-11-11)
claims.quote: display a higher degree of stylistic uniformity, clustering tightly by model

claims.claim: 11,800 gpt-4o-mini stories for 236 nationalities conform to a single small-town, return-to-tradition, community-event plot with conflict sanitised and tension downplayed.
claims.source: Rettberg & Wigers (arXiv 2507.22445, Jul 2025)
claims.quote: Real-world conflicts are sanitised, romance is almost absent

claims.claim: AI stories prioritise stability, nostalgia and reconciliation over change, a form of narrative standardisation distinct from representational bias.
claims.source: Rettberg & Wigers (arXiv 2507.22445)
claims.quote: prioritises stability above change

claims.claim: LLM rewriting of personal narratives removes contractions, first-person pronouns, function words and emotion words while raising word length and vocabulary diversity, shifting embedded narration toward distanced narration even under voice-preserving prompts.
claims.source: van Nuenen, Voice Under Revision (arXiv 2604.22142, Apr 2026)
claims.quote: from embedded to distanced narration

claims.claim: Professional authors' CREATIVITY INDEX (share of text not reconstructible from web n-grams) is 66.2% higher than LLMs', and RLHF alignment lowers LLMs' index by 30.1%.
claims.source: Lu, Sclar, Hallinan, Mireshghallah et al., AI as Humanity's Salieri (arXiv 2410.04265)
claims.quote: on average 66.2% higher than that of LLMs

claims.claim: Instruction-tuned models use present participial clauses 2–5x the human rate (GPT-4o 5.3x, d=1.38), e.g. 'Bryan, leaning on his agility, dances around the ring'.
claims.source: Reinhart, Markey, Laudenbach, Pantusen, Yurko, Weinberg & Brown, PNAS 122 (2025-02-25)

claims.claim: Instruction-tuned LLMs use nominalizations 1.5–2x, 'that' subject clauses 2.6x and phrasal coordination 1.9x human rates, producing a noun-heavy academic style regardless of genre.
claims.source: Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025
claims.quote: informationally dense, noun-heavy style

claims.claim: GPT-4o uses camaraderie 162x, tapestry 155x, intricate 119x, underscore 107x, amidst 100x human rates; GPT-4o-mini palpable 145x; words that connote complex relations produce hollow summative sentences.
claims.source: Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025
claims.quote: grandiose, if hollow, summative sentences

claims.claim: LLMs fail to vary style by genre or context the way humans do, so fiction-appropriate words become conspicuous elsewhere and the same style is applied everywhere.
claims.source: Reinhart et al., PNAS 2025
claims.quote: do not vary their linguistic output in response to contextual factors

claims.claim: Professional writers editing 1,057 LLM paragraphs spent 28% of edits on awkward word choice, 20% on poor sentence structure, 18% on unnecessary/redundant exposition and 17% on clichés, plus purple prose, lack of specificity and tense slips.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Laban & Wu, Can AI writing be salvaged? (CHI 2025; arXiv 2409.14509)
claims.quote: Writer-edited > LLM-edited > LLM-generated

claims.claim: LLM prose repeats templates such as 'sense of', 'weight of', 'mix of', and the word 'unspoken' appears in about 15% of LLM outputs but rarely in human samples.
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Laban & Wu (CHI 2025)

claims.feature: no model family is better at prose
claims.claim: Writers saw no significant quality difference among GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Llama-3.1-70b, and fiction scored lower (4.5) than creative nonfiction (5.0–5.2).
claims.source: Chakrabarty, Laban & Wu (CHI 2025)
claims.quote: writers perceived no significant qualitative differences

claims.claim: Idiosyncratic plot elements recur across many samples from the same prompt (50/100 continuations 'take the second left', 16/100 a bakery) and even across models, while human plot elements sit in the tail or outside the LLM distribution.
claims.source: Xu, Jojic, Rao, Brockett & Dolan, Echoes in AI (PNAS 2025-09-02; arXiv 2501.00273)
claims.quote: plot elements that are echoed across a number of generations

claims.claim: LLM stories show 7–9x higher 'drop ratios' than human stories, meaning a suspenseful element is resolved immediately after it peaks instead of being developed.
claims.source: Xu et al., Echoes in AI (PNAS 2025)

claims.claim: GPT-4 stories are Man-in-a-Hole over half the time and Rags-to-Riches 13.0% (humans 4.4%), while Riches-to-Rags (1.3% vs 14.6%) and Oedipus (1.7% vs 9.3%) arcs nearly vanish.
claims.source: Tian, Huang, Liu, Jiang, Spangher, Chen, May & Peng (EMNLP 2024; arXiv 2407.13248)
claims.quote: strongly favoring positive outcomes

claims.claim: Major Setback and Climax arrive about 10–15% earlier in GPT-4 narratives, and human stories sustain higher suspense with the gap widening from midpoint to end.
claims.source: Tian et al. (EMNLP 2024)
claims.quote: higher levels of suspense

claims.claim: By the 100-Endings metric, professional New Yorker fiction stays unpredictable near the close (no-rate 0.607) while top LLM stories collapse to 0.215, retaining only 23% of tension peaks versus 52%.
claims.source: Sui, Zhu, Cheng, West, So, Long & Holtzman, Spoiler Alert (arXiv 2604.09854, Apr 2026)
claims.quote: fundamental inability to defer closure

claims.claim: EQ-Bench rubric scores rank LLM stories (81–84) above New Yorker stories (78.71) even though the LLM stories are far more predictable.
claims.source: Sui et al., Spoiler Alert (arXiv 2604.09854)

claims.claim: Across 28 LLMs, human story continuations are 2–4x more surprising (perplexity ratios 2.76–8.82x); instruction tuning widens the gap and the gap is 25–30% larger in fiction than in essays or news.
claims.source: Sui, LLMs Exhibit Significantly Lower Uncertainty in Creative Writing (arXiv 2602.16162, Feb 2026)
claims.quote: trite, repetitive, overly verbose, and cliché-ridden

claims.claim: Moving from base to SFT to DPO to RLVR checkpoints makes thematic transitions more uniform, replaces high-intensity emotion with neutrality and shrinks stylistic diversity, most severely against professional literary fiction.
claims.source: Li, Zhu, Wu, Bao & Evans, Narrative Flattening (arXiv 2605.27878, May 2026)
claims.quote: High-intensity emotions give way to neutrality

claims.claim: LLM story character networks are denser (0.338–0.470 vs 0.182), more positive (mean edge weight 0.236–0.659 vs −0.061) and more clustered than human science-fiction, with far less variability.
claims.source: Nonaka & Perry (arXiv 2510.18932, Sep 2025)
claims.quote: less conflict-driven social dynamics

claims.claim: GPT stories open 'Once upon a time' in a vague futuristic place and close with a moral lesson in stock phrases, while crowdworker stories open on tension and vary far more.
claims.source: Beguš, Experimental Narratives (HSSC 2024; arXiv 2310.12902)
claims.quote: proneness to wrapping up each story with a moral lesson

claims.claim: Human evaluation of LLM fiction shows a 'high-starting, low-ending' pattern: strong openings that deteriorate.
claims.source: Wang, Gao, Hu & Wan, Towards a Novel Benchmark (Findings ACL 2025)
claims.quote: high-starting, low-ending

claims.claim: Across 10 LLMs, generated narratives are consistently more similar to each other than human stories are, and negative prompting or temperature scaling do not fix it.
claims.source: DK & Hatzel, Do LLMs Always Tell the Same Stories? (arXiv 2606.17350)
claims.quote: fail to meaningfully address this homogeneity

claims.claim: Under constraint-based selection, six LLMs consistently choose stylistic elements over event, character and setting content.
claims.source: Jung, Choi, Chae & Jung, Style over Story (ACL 2026; arXiv 2510.02025)
claims.quote: models consistently prioritize Style over narrative content elements

claims.claim: LLMs produce mood-laden 'perceived space' at about twice the human rate (GPT-4.1 0.47 vs human 0.19) and under-produce action space, substituting atmosphere for embodied movement.
claims.source: Rohrbacher et al., How LLMs Build Fictional Worlds (arXiv 2609.02482, Sep 2026)
claims.quote: roughly twice the human baseline

claims.claim: In long LLM stories, consistency errors concentrate in factual and temporal dimensions, around the middle of the narrative and in high-entropy segments (no human baseline).
claims.source: Li, Guo, Wu, Lee, Li & Xie, Lost in Stories (arXiv 2603.05890)
claims.quote: most common in factual and temporal dimensions

claims.claim: Baseline ChatGPT stories lose to psychologically planned stories on suspense 84.9% of the time in human judgments.
claims.source: Xie & Riedl, Creating Suspenseful Stories (arXiv 2402.17119)
claims.quote: poor understanding of story suspense

claims.claim: Replicating four suspense-perception studies, LMs can tell a text is meant to be suspenseful but cannot estimate relative suspense or its rise and fall like human readers.
claims.source: Matlin et al. (arXiv 2508.15794)
claims.quote: do not process suspense in the same way as human readers

claims.claim: Across 20,000 stories from four models, Elias appears in 26.5%, Mara 16.7%, Elara 13.1% and a lighthouse in 51.2%; 88.3% contain at least one of 11 core tokens, with Elias 900x its rate in published fiction.
claims.source: Hamilton & Mimno, Elias in the Lighthouse, Again? (arXiv 2605.26492, May 2026)
claims.quote: 900 times more frequent in our corpus

claims.claim: Each model family defaults to fixed character-name pairs (Claude: Elena Vasquez + Marcus Chen; Gemini: Aris Thorne + Lena Petrova; GPT: Elara Voss).
claims.source: Brzozowski & Chung, The Ghost Couple (arXiv 2606.02184)
claims.quote: co-occurrence rates far exceed chance

claims.claim: LLMs show a strong bias toward literal, explicit communication, producing literal clues 60% of the time in a subtext game.
claims.source: Ahuja, Li & Lampinen, Beneath the Surface (arXiv 2604.05273)
claims.quote: strong bias towards overly literal, explicit communication

claims.claim: Six literary experts scored Patricio Pron's synopses 1.94 on creativity vs GPT-4's 0.97 (English) and 0.88 (Spanish), and style originality 1.70 vs 0.63/0.36.
claims.source: Marco, Gonzalo, Mateo-Girona & del Castillo, Pron vs Prompt (EMNLP 2024; arXiv 2407.01119)
claims.quote: GPT-4 receives predominantly scores of 0/1, while Pron receives mostly 2/3

claims.claim: Experts found GPT-4 texts clichéd, moralising, formulaic and indistinguishable from one another, with forced or hollow endings, and learned to recognise them with exposure.
claims.source: Marco et al., Pron vs Prompt (EMNLP 2024)

claims.claim: Non-expert readers reward readability and textual richness while experts weight thematic development, rhetorical variety and sentiment dynamics, explaining contradictory AI-writing evaluations.
claims.source: Marco, Gonzalo & Fresno, The Reader is the Metric (arXiv 2506.03310)
claims.quote: thematic development, rhetorical variety, and sentiment dynamics

claims.claim: GPT-4o synopses contained clichés only 26.7% of the time but surprising associations in just 1.6%, versus 15% for a fine-tuned BART.
claims.source: Marco, Rello & Gonzalo (COLING 2025; arXiv 2409.11547)
claims.quote: more predictable and formulaic narratives

claims.claim: 1,634 non-experts identified AI poems at 46.6% (below chance), judged them more human than human poems and rated them higher on rhythm and beauty, apparently misreading human complexity as incoherence.
claims.source: Porter & Machery, Scientific Reports 14:26133 (2024-11-14)
claims.quote: poetry experience did not improve discrimination performance

claims.claim: Five heavy ChatGPT users' majority vote misclassified 1 of 300 articles, citing 'AI vocabulary' plus formality, originality and clarity, and stayed robust to paraphrase and humanization.
claims.source: Russell, Karpinska & Iyyer (ACL 2025; arXiv 2501.15654)
claims.quote: misclassifies only 1 of 300 articles

claims.source: Gómez-Rodríguez & Williams, A Confederacy of Models (Findings EMNLP 2023)
claims.quote: Humans retain an edge in creativity

claims.claim: Humor splits LLMs into those that manage it comparably to humans and those that fail outright (GPT-3.5 3.3/10 vs humans 6.4).
claims.source: Gómez-Rodríguez & Williams (Findings EMNLP 2023)

claims.claim: Slop is fluent but generic, verbose and low-density text; relevance, density and tone best predict human slop judgments, and frontier LLM judges show near-zero agreement with human annotators.

claims.quote: generic, overly verbose, inaccurate, irrelevant to its intended purpose

claims.claim: LLM sentences cluster in a 10–30 token band with less length variation than human sentences, and lexical richness is lower (STTR 0.424 vs 0.491).

claims.quote: less variation when compared to human-generated sentences

claims.claim: LLM text carries more joy and positive emotion while humans show more fear and disgust; LLMs also use more pronouns and magnify male-pronoun bias.
claims.source: Muñoz-Ortiz et al. 2024

claims.claim: Human sentence lengths show a broader, flatter distribution while AI outputs cluster around the mean; AI cuts informal expressions 54–72%, raises positive emotion 114–133% and certainty 111–152%.
claims.source: Rodrigues, Sturm & Pinheiro, iScience (Feb 2026)
claims.quote: broader and flatter distribution

claims.claim: ChatGPT speeches overuse nouns, possessives and numbers, underuse verbs, pronouns and adverbs, and read as too standardised compared with real presidential addresses.
claims.source: Labbé, Labbé & Savoy (arXiv 2411.18382)
claims.quote: too standardized sentences

claims.claim: GPT-4o imitating Hemingway produced lexical diversity of 47.79 versus Hemingway's 34.62, and its function-word profile overlapped generic GPT output rather than the author's fingerprint.
claims.source: Mikros, Digital Scholarship in the Humanities 40(2), 2025
claims.quote: significant overlap with generic GPT outputs

claims.claim: LLM argumentative prose uses tricolon 7.13 per document versus 3.73 for human experts, suppresses rhetorical questions (2.28 vs 5.55), doubles performed hesitancy and distributes devices with template-like uniformity.
claims.source: Bakhshi, Saying More Than They Know (arXiv 2604.19768, Mar 2026)
claims.quote: deployed independently of argumentative occasion

claims.claim: Writing with InstructGPT raised corpus homogenization (0.1536 to 0.1660) and repeated higher-order n-grams, with the loss traced to model-contributed text rather than changed writer behaviour.
claims.source: Padmakumar & He (ICLR 2024; arXiv 2309.05196)
claims.quote: repeat higher-order n-grams more frequently

claims.claim: Users brainstorming with ChatGPT produced less semantically distinct ideas across users than with an alternative tool, while feeling less responsible for them.
claims.source: Anderson, Shah & Kreminski (Creativity & Cognition 2024; arXiv 2402.01536)
claims.quote: less semantically distinct ideas with ChatGPT

claims.claim: Across 22 LLMs and 102 humans, LLM response variability is far lower (AUT 0.459 vs 0.699; DAT 0.632 vs 0.791), so switching models does not restore diversity.

claims.quote: much more similar to other LLM responses

claims.quote: 702 (61%) state a preference for human-written dialogue

claims.claim: 32% of GPT-4 game lines were judged illogical once the next utterance appeared, and generations violated the game's faction logic (e.g. an 'ultra-liberal' character).

claims.quote: illogical in hindsight

claims.feature: script dialogue: literal and on the nose

claims.quote: on the nose, pun names

claims.claim: Professionals found character journeys unfinished and emotional motivation missing, with logic gaps and repetitive generation loops.

claims.quote: lack of thematic focus, out-of-character dialogue, and insufficient character development

claims.claim: Industry experts building a game-narrative quality framework record LLM outputs as unconvincing, repetitive or tonally misaligned, with overly positive or uninspired endings and genre-adherence failures.

claims.quote: overly positive or uninspired endings

claims.claim: In 200 gpt-4o-mini vs 200 human WritingPrompts stories, human sentiment spikes in the last tenth while AI stories climb from the 70% mark and resolve repeatedly.

claims.quote: the story seems to end, then it ends again

claims.page: After Editing Two AI-Assisted Manuscripts, I Rewrote My Client Agreement

claims.claim: With no human author behind the text there is no intent for an editor to serve, which makes AI-generated manuscripts harder, not easier, to edit.

claims.quote: There's no human on the other end

claims.claim: AI dialogue gives no character verbal tics, dialect, or a pattern of evasion; everyone says what they mean, and mysteries get resolved by as-you-know-Bob speech rather than action.

claims.page: I Asked the Machine to Tell on Itself: A Field Guide to AI Tells

claims.claim: AI stories carry philosophical, expository dialogue 59% of the time versus 34% in human stories.

claims.page: I Asked the Machine to Tell on Itself: A Field Guide to AI Tells
claims.quote: No grain: no proper nouns, no specific months, no brand names.

claims.claim: AI cannot build meaning by accumulating repeated specific observations across a manuscript, and it describes emotions rather than showing them through behavior.

claims.claim: AI prose stays in shallow point of view, avoids concrete sensory detail, and delivers emotions disconnected from the trigger that should have produced them.

claims.page: What Makes a Story "Look" Like AI Wrote It?
claims.quote: It will fail to have the emotion linked to it

claims.claim: Fiction is roughly one deliberate choice per word; a prompt makes far fewer choices, and the unmade choices come out generic and without intention.

Her original publishers hated them; they scrubbed her poems clean... Later editors put the dashes back -- because they weren't accidents. They were architecture.' Tool-versus-intent half is the Dickinson coda: her editors 'mistook unfamiliar form for flawed thinking... the dash wasn't excess. It was intention.' Page calls Dickinson 'the patron saint of the em dash' rather than saying it was her signature mark.

223.trueWording: em dash still far outstrips the semi-colon and exclamation mark
223.note: SALT.agency, Sarah Mitchell, January 29, 2026. The supplied quote IS on the page word for word, but it supports a DIFFERENT point (detector unreliability), not the Ngram claim -- so it cannot be cited as evidence for this claim. The Ngram substance is on the page: a 'Google Books Ngram graph comparing the frequencies of the em dash (in blue), semi-colon (red) and exclamation point (green) in books published between 1500 and 2022', plus 'precious little evidence that ChatGPT does use the em dash too frequently; or at least more frequently than the average professional writer' and the training-data argument about professionally edited pre-internet text. Re-cut the claim to the dominance wording.
223.unsupportedLimb: "em dash frequency has stayed high for centuries" is contradicted — the page states usage "does drop away after the mid-'90s"; only relative dominance survives (and the supplied quote supports detector unreliability, a different point).

224.note: Robert Roy Britt, The Writer's Guide, Jul 28, 2026, 'AI's Assault on the Em Dash Should Worry All Writers'. Quote verbatim ('You see, em dashes aren't the problem.' and again later). 225.note: Quote exact.
